To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of inappropriate antibiotic prescription for respiratory indications was 15% (95% CI: 14% to 16%) in children and 21% (95%CI: 21% to 22%) in adults.
(1) the prevalence of inappropriate antibiotic prescription is higher than expected; (2) the most prominent inappropriate antibiotic prescription for respiratory indications is in adult patients; and
the prevalence of antibiotic prescriptions for respiratory tract infections (RTIs) in general practice is high and that the prescription of broad-spectrum antibiotics for RTIs is common.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods and algorithms for the analysis of large-scale biological data sets.
the development of an efficient and effective approach to antibiotic stewardship.
the development of a novel, efficient, and cost-effective method for the preparation of a series of 3-aryl-2,3-dihydroquinazolin-4(1H)-ones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
antibiotic prescription for respiratory indications is inappropriate in 10-30% of cases.
the antibiotic use in the Netherlands has been reduced, especially in children, and that there is no evidence of increased antibiotic resistance as a consequence.
antibiotic prescribing in primary care is generally appropriate and in accordance with the guidelines.

we have demonstrated that antibiotic prescription for respiratory indications in the primary care setting is often inappropriate.
the most prominent risk factor for inappropriate antibiotic prescription is adult age.

The main takeaway from our work is that
antibiotic prescribing for respiratory tract indications is still high, and that this prescribing is more common for adults than for children.
antibiotic use for respiratory tract infections is inappropriate in a large proportion of adult and pediatric patients, with a higher proportion of inappropriate use in adults.
the majority of antibiotics prescribed in primary care are inappropriate.
